claim: Bacterial adaptation to antibiotic combinations depends on the joint inhibitory effects of the two drugs (drug interaction) and how resistance to one drug impacts resistance to the other (collateral effects).
source: Bacterial adaptation to antibiotic combinations depends on the joint inhibitory effects of the two drugs (drug interaction [DI]) and how resistance to one drug impacts resistance to the other (collateral effects [CE]).
evidence: This is a foundational claim stated in the abstract that frames the entire study.

claim: Evolved resistance to component drugs is governed by a Price equation whose covariance terms encode geometric features of both the two-drug-response surface and the correlations between resistance levels to those drugs.
source: We show that evolved resistance to the component drugs – and in turn, the adaptation of growth rate – is governed by a Price equation whose covariance terms encode geometric features of both the two-drug-response surface (DI) in ancestral cells and the correlations between resistance levels to those drugs (CE).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study presented in the abstract and demonstrated through mathematical modeling.

claim: Mean evolutionary trajectories reduce to a type of weighted gradient dynamics, with the drug interaction dictating the shape of the underlying landscape and the collateral effects constraining the motion on those landscapes.
source: Within this framework, mean evolutionary trajectories reduce to a type of weighted gradient dynamics, with the drug interaction dictating the shape of the underlying landscape and the collateral effects constraining the motion on those landscapes.
evidence: This is a key theoretical result derived from the Price equation framework presented in the study.

claim: Constraints on available mutational pathways can be incorporated into the framework, adding a third key driver of evolution.
source: We also demonstrate how constraints on available mutational pathways can be incorporated into the framework, adding a third key driver of evolution.
evidence: This is stated as an extension of the model demonstrated in the study.

claim: Specific dosage combinations can shift the weighting of drug interactions and collateral effects, leading to different and temporally explicit selective outcomes.
source: Our results clarify the complex relationship between drug interactions and collateral effects in multidrug environments and illustrate how specific dosage combinations can shift the weighting of these two effects, leading to different and temporally explicit selective outcomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results presented in the study.

claim: Antibiotic resistance represents a rapid rise and practical public health threat.
source: These challenges represent open theoretical questions but also underlie practical public health threats – exemplified by the rapid rise of antibiotic resistance (Davies and Davies, 2010; Levy and Marshall, 2004) – where evolutionary dynamics are fundamental to the challenge, and perhaps, to the solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on antibiotic resistance.

claim: Evolution-based strategies for impeding drug resistance have gained significant attention in recent years.
source: In recent years, evolution-based strategies for impeding drug resistance have gained significant attention.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the extensive list of citations that follows.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity can modulate resistance evolution.
source: These approaches have identified a number of different factors that could modulate resistance evolution, including spatial heterogeneity (Zhang et al., 2011; Baym et al., 2016a; Greulich et al., 2012; Hermsen et al., 2012; Moreno-Gamez et al., 2015; Gokhale et al., 2018; De Jong and Wood, 2018; Santos-Lopez et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Competitive interactions between bacterial cells can modulate resistance evolution.
source: These approaches have identified a number of different factors that could modulate resistance evolution, including spatial heterogeneity (Zhang et al., 2011; Baym et al., 2016a; Greulich et al., 2012; Hermsen et al., 2012; Moreno-Gamez et al., 2015; Gokhale et al., 2018; De Jong and Wood, 2018; Santos-Lopez et al., 2019); competitive (Read et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2020), cooperative (Meredith et al., 2015b; Artemova et al., 2015; Sorg et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2012; Karslake et al., 2016; Yurtsev et al., 2016; Hallinen et al., 2020), or metabolic (Adamowicz et al., 2018; Adamowicz et al., 2020) interactions between bacterial cells
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cooperative interactions between bacterial cells can modulate resistance evolution.
source: These approaches have identified a number of different factors that could modulate resistance evolution, including spatial heterogeneity (Zhang et al., 2011; Baym et al., 2016a; Greulich et al., 2012; Hermsen et al., 2012; Moreno-Gamez et al., 2015; Gokhale et al., 2018; De Jong and Wood, 2018; Santos-Lopez et al., 2019); competitive (Read et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2020), cooperative (Meredith et al., 2015b; Artemova et al., 2015; Sorg et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2012; Karslake et al., 2016; Yurtsev et al., 2016; Hallinen et al., 2020), or metabolic (Adamowicz et al., 2018; Adamowicz et al., 2020) interactions between bacterial cells
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Metabolic interactions between bacterial cells can modulate resistance evolution.
source: These approaches have identified a number of different factors that could modulate resistance evolution, including spatial heterogeneity (Zhang et al., 2011; Baym et al., 2016a; Greulich et al., 2012; Hermsen et al., 2012; Moreno-Gamez et al., 2015; Gokhale et al., 2018; De Jong and Wood, 2018; Santos-Lopez et al., 2019); competitive (Read et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2020), cooperative (Meredith et al., 2015b; Artemova et al., 2015; Sorg et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2012; Karslake et al., 2016; Yurtsev et al., 2016; Hallinen et al., 2020), or metabolic (Adamowicz et al., 2018; Adamowicz et al., 2020) interactions between bacterial cells
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synergy with the immune system can modulate resistance evolution, especially in the context of adaptive treatment.
source: synergy with the immune system, especially in the context of adaptive treatment (Gjini and Brito, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Epistasis between resistance mutations can modulate resistance evolution.
source: epistasis between resistance mutations (Trindade et al., 2009; Borrell et al., 2013; Lukačišinová et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Plasmid dynamics can modulate resistance evolution.
source: plasmid dynamics (Lopatkin et al., 2016; Lopatkin et al., 2017; Cooper et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Precise tuning of drug doses can modulate resistance evolution.
source: precise tuning of drug doses (Lipsitch and Levin, 1997; Yoshida et al., 2017; Meredith et al., 2015a; Nichol et al., 2015; Fuentes-Hernandez et al., 2015; Coates et al., 2018; Iram et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cycling or mixing drugs at the hospital level can modulate resistance evolution.
source: cycling or mixing drugs at the hospital level (Bergstrom et al., 2004; Beardmore et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Statistical correlations between resistance profiles for different drugs can modulate resistance evolution.
source: statistical correlations between resistance profiles for different drugs (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Kim et al., 2014; Pál et al., 2015; Barbosa et al., 2017; Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015; Nichol et al., 2019; Podnecky et al., 2018; Imamovic et al., 2018; Barbosa et al., 2019; Rosenkilde et al., 2019; Apjok et al., 2019; Maltas and Wood, 2019; Maltas et al., 2020; Hernando-Amado et al., 2020; Roemhild et al., 2020; Ardell and Kryazhimskiy, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior work.

claim: Drug combinations are a particularly promising approach for slowing resistance.
source: Drug combinations are a particularly promising approach for slowing resistance (Baym et al., 2016b), but the evolutionary impacts of combination therapy remain difficult to predict, especially in a clinical setting (Podolsky, 2015; Woods and Read, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The evolutionary impacts of combination therapy remain difficult to predict, especially in a clinical setting.
source: Drug combinations are a particularly promising approach for slowing resistance (Baym et al., 2016b), but the evolutionary impacts of combination therapy remain difficult to predict, especially in a clinical setting (Podolsky, 2015; Woods and Read, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Antibiotics are said to interact when the combined effect of the drugs is greater than (synergy) or less than (antagonism) expected based on the effects of the drugs alone.
source: Antibiotics are said to interact when the combined effect of the drugs is greater than (synergy) or less than (antagonism) expected based on the effects of the drugs alone (Greco et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to established pharmacology literature.

claim: Drug interactions can accelerate, reduce, or even reverse the evolution of resistance.
source: But these interactions can also accelerate, reduce, or even reverse the evolution of resistance (Chait et al., 2007; Michel et al., 2008; Hegreness et al., 2008; Pena-Miller et al., 2013; Dean et al., 2020), leading to tradeoffs between short-term inhibitory effects and long-term evolutionary potential (Torella et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Drug interactions lead to tradeoffs between short-term inhibitory effects and long-term evolutionary potential.
source: But these interactions can also accelerate, reduce, or even reverse the evolution of resistance (Chait et al., 2007; Michel et al., 2008; Hegreness et al., 2008; Pena-Miller et al., 2013; Dean et al., 2020), leading to tradeoffs between short-term inhibitory effects and long-term evolutionary potential (Torella et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Resistance to one drug may be associated with modulated resistance to other drugs (cross-resistance or collateral sensitivity).
source: In addition, resistance to one drug may be associated with modulated resistance to other drugs. This cross-resistance (or collateral sensitivity) between drugs in a combination has also been shown to significantly modulate resistance evolution (Barbosa et al., 2018; Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015; Munck et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cross-resistance or collateral sensitivity between drugs in a combination has been shown to significantly modulate resistance evolution.
source: This cross-resistance (or collateral sensitivity) between drugs in a combination has also been shown to significantly modulate resistance evolution (Barbosa et al., 2018; Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015; Munck et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adaptation to a drug combination may often reflect both drug interactions and collateral effects.
source: Yet adaptation to a drug combination may often reflect both phenomena, with the pleiotropic effects that couple resistance to individual drugs constraining, or constrained by, the interactions that occur when those drugs are used simultaneously.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim that motivates the study.

claim: The underlying genotype space is high-dimensional and potentially rugged, rendering the genotypic trajectories prohibitively complex.
source: In addition, the underlying genotype space is high-dimensional and potentially rugged, rendering the genotypic trajectories prohibitively complex (de Visser and Krug, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on evolutionary dynamics.

claim: The model leverages scaling relations between the drug-response surfaces of ancestral and mutant populations.
source: In this work, we attempt to navigate these obstacles by modeling evolutionary dynamics on lower-dimensional phenotype spaces that leverage scaling relations between the drug-response surfaces of ancestral and mutant populations.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: Multiobjective evolutionary optimization may occur on surprisingly low-dimensional phenotypic spaces.
source: Our approach is inspired by the fact that multiobjective evolutionary optimization may occur on surprisingly low-dimensional phenotypic spaces (Shoval et al., 2012; Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The model associates selectable resistance traits with changes in effective drug concentrations.
source: To develop a similarly coarse-grained picture of multidrug resistance, we associate selectable resistance traits with changes in effective drug concentrations, formalizing the geometric rescaling assumptions originally pioneered in Chait et al., 2007; Hegreness et al., 2008; Michel et al., 2008 and connecting evolutionary dynamics with a simple measurable property of ancestral populations.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach building on prior work.

claim: In some cases, the effective concentration change corresponds to a physical change in intracellular drug concentration due to efflux pumps or drug degrading enzymes.
source: In some cases – for example, resistance due to efflux pumps (Wood and Cluzel, 2012) or drug degrading enzymes (Yurtsev et al., 2013) – this effective concentration change corresponds to a physical change in intracellular drug concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similar rescaling arguments were originally proposed in Chait et al., 2007.
source: Similar rescaling arguments were originally proposed in Chait et al., 2007, where they were used to predict correlations between the rate of resistance evolution and the type of drug interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rescaling arguments have been used to describe fitness tradeoffs during adaptation.
source: These arguments have also been used to describe fitness tradeoffs during adaptation (Das et al., 2020) and to account for more general changes in the dose-response curves, though in many cases the original two-parameter rescaling was sufficient to describe the growth surface in mutants (Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In many cases, the original two-parameter rescaling was sufficient to describe the growth surface in mutants.
source: These arguments have also been used to describe fitness tradeoffs during adaptation (Das et al., 2020) and to account for more general changes in the dose-response curves, though in many cases the original two-parameter rescaling was sufficient to describe the growth surface in mutants (Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When only a single drug is used, rescaling leads to a simple relationship between the characteristic inhibitory concentrations of the ancestral and mutant populations.
source: When only a single drug is used, this rescaling leads to a simple relationship between the characteristic inhibitory concentrations – for example, the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) or the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) – of the ancestral (sensitive) and mutant (resistant) populations.
evidence: This is a consequence of the rescaling model explained in the text.

claim: In the presence of two drugs, rescaling corresponds to a shape-preserving rescaling of the contours of constant growth.
source: In the presence of two drugs, the dose-response curves become dose-response surfaces, and rescaling now corresponds to a shape-preserving rescaling of the contours of constant growth.
evidence: This is an extension of the single-drug rescaling concept to two drugs.

claim: Equation 5 is an example of the Price equation from evolutionary biology.
source: Equation 5 is an example of the well-known Price equation from evolutionary biology (Price, 1970; Price, 1972; Frank, 1995; Lehtonen et al., 2020), which says that the change in the (population) mean value of a trait is governed by the covariance of traits and fitness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on the Price equation.

claim: The Price equation states that the change in the population mean value of a trait is governed by the covariance of traits and fitness.
source: Equation 5 is an example of the well-known Price equation from evolutionary biology (Price, 1970; Price, 1972; Frank, 1995; Lehtonen et al., 2020), which says that the change in the (population) mean value of a trait is governed by the covariance of traits and fitness.
evidence: This is a statement of the Price equation principle.

claim: The Price equation is not a mathematical model in the traditional sense, but a mathematical statement describing the statistical relationship between variables.
source: In what follows, we will sometimes casually refer to Equation 5 as a 'model,' but it is important to note that the Price equation is not, in and of itself, a mathematical model in the traditional sense. Instead, it is a simple mathematical statement describing the statistical relationship between variables, which are themselves defined in some underlying model.
evidence: This is a clarification about the nature of the Price equation.

claim: Equation 5 encodes dynamics that depend on both the interaction between drugs and the collateral effects of resistance.
source: Equation 5 encodes deceptively rich dynamics that depend on both the interaction between drugs and the collateral effects of resistance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Price equation in the context of the model.

claim: Constraints on scaling parameters correspond to correlations between resistance levels to different drugs (cross-resistance or collateral sensitivity).
source: These constraints correspond to correlations between resistance levels to different drugs – that is, to cross-resistance (when pairs of scaling parameters simultaneously increase resistance to both drugs) or to collateral sensitivity (when one scaling parameter leads to increased resistance and the other to increased sensitivity).
evidence: This is a definition of how collateral effects are represented in the model.

claim: The evolution of the scaling parameters is determined by both the drug interaction and the collateral effects, quantified by the covariance between rescaled trait values and the ancestral dose-response surface.
source: The evolution of the scaling parameters is not determined solely by the drug interaction or by the collateral effects, but instead by both – quantified by the covariance between these rescaled trait values and the ancestral dose-response surface.
evidence: This is a key conceptual insight from the model.

claim: The model describes both the dynamics of the scaling parameters and the dynamics of growth rate adaptation in the population as a whole.
source: The model therefore describes both the dynamics of the scaling parameters, which describe how resistance to each drug changes over time (Figure 2C), and the dynamics of growth rate adaptation in the population as a whole (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Selection is determined by both the drug interaction and the collateral effects, consistent with previous experimental findings.
source: This rescaling model indicates that selection is determined by both the drug interaction and the collateral effects, consistent with previous experimental findings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model that is consistent with prior work.

claim: Cross-resistance leads to rapid increases in resistance to both drugs and the fastest growth adaptation in the example shown.
source: In this example, cross-resistance (pink) leads to rapid increases in resistance to both drugs (rapid decreases in scaling parameters, Figure 3C, D) and the fastest growth adaptation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a result from numerical simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: If resistance is limited primarily to one drug, growth adaptation is slowed.
source: By contrast, if resistance is limited primarily to one drug (cyan or black), growth adaptation is slowed (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is a result from numerical simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Purely horizontal or purely vertical motion in the space of scaling parameters leads to only a modest change in growth because the underlying response surface is relatively flat in those directions.
source: intuitively, purely horizontal or purely vertical motion in the space of scaling parameters leads to only a modest change in growth because the underlying response surface is relatively flat in those directions, meaning that the rescaled concentration, in each case, lies near the original contour (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an intuitive explanation of the simulation results illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Resistance to both drugs can develop at approximately the same rate even when collateral structure suggests resistance to one drug will dominate, due to the contour shapes (drug interaction).
source: As a result of the contour shapes (drug interaction), resistance to both drugs can develop at approximately the same rate (for example), even when collateral structure suggests resistance to one drug will dominate (e.g., cyan case in Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results in Figure 3.

claim: When both collateral effects and drug interactions vary, the dynamics can be considerably more complex.
source: When both collateral effects and drug interactions vary, the dynamics can be considerably more complex, and the dominant driver of adaptation can be drug interaction, collateral effects, or a combination of both.
evidence: This is a general statement about the model behavior.

claim: Previous studies support that adaptation has been observed to be driven primarily by drug interactions, primarily by collateral effects, or by combinations of both.
source: Previous studies support this picture as adaptation has been observed to be driven primarily by drug interactions (Chait et al., 2007; Michel et al., 2008; Hegreness et al., 2008), primarily by collateral effects (Munck et al., 2014; Barbosa et al., 2018), or by combinations of both (Baym et al., 2016b; Barbosa et al., 2018; Dean et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: In the absence of both drug interactions (linear isoboles) and collateral effects (uncorrelated scaling parameters), adaptation is slower when the drugs are used in combination than when they are used alone.
source: In the absence of both drug interactions (linear isoboles) and collateral effects (uncorrelated scaling parameters), adaptation is slower when the drugs are used in combination than when they are used alone, consistent with the fact that adaptation to multiple stressors is expected to take longer than adaptation to each stressor alone (Figure 4; middle row, middle column).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Modulating collateral effects with drug interaction fixed can have dramatic impacts on adaptation.
source: As in Figure 3, modulating collateral effects with drug interaction fixed can have dramatic impacts on adaptation (Figure 4, columns).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Modulating the drug interaction in the absence of collateral effects will significantly impact adaptation, with synergistic interactions leading to accelerated adaptation relative to other types of drug interaction.
source: On the other hand, modulating the drug interaction in the absence of collateral effects will also significantly impact adaptation, with synergistic interactions leading to accelerated adaptation relative to other types of drug interaction (Figure 4, middle row; compare green curves across row).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Similar interaction-driven adaptation has been observed in multiple bacterial species.
source: Similar interaction-driven adaptation has been observed in multiple bacterial species (Chait et al., 2007; Michel et al., 2008; Hegreness et al., 2008; Dean et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Equation 9 provides an accurate description of the full dynamics across a wide range of conditions.
source: Equation 9 provides an accurate description of the full dynamics across a wide range of conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and has a surprisingly simple interpretation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adaptation dynamics are driven by a type of weighted gradient dynamics on the response surface, with the weighting determined by the correlation coefficients describing resistance levels to the two drugs.
source: Adaptation dynamics are driven by a type of weighted gradient dynamics on the response surface, with the weighting determined by the correlation coefficients describing resistance levels to the two drugs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of Equation 9.

claim: In the absence of constraints on the available scaling parameters, adaptation follows the gradient of the response surface to rapidly achieve increased fitness.
source: That is, in the absence of constraints on the available scaling parameters, adaptation follows the gradient of the response surface to rapidly achieve increased fitness, and because the response surface defines the type of drug interaction, that interaction governs the rate of adaptation.
evidence: This is an explanation of the gradient dynamics in the absence of collateral effects.

claim: The model predicts different trajectories for different external doses, leading to dramatically different changes in resistance and growth rate adaptation.
source: The model predicts different trajectories for different external doses (selective regimes: red to blue, Figure 5, top panel), leading to dramatically different changes in resistance (IC50) and growth rate adaptation (Figure 5, bottom panels), similar to those observed in experiment.
evidence: This is a result from comparing model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The model predicts a dramatic decrease in CIP resistance as TGC concentration is increased along a contour of constant growth, which is confirmed by experiments.
source: Specifically, the model predicts (and experiments confirm) a dramatic decrease in CIP resistance as TGC concentration is increased along a contour of constant growth.
evidence: This is a specific prediction of the model that is validated by experimental data.

claim: As TGC eclipses a critical concentration of approximately 0.025 g/mL, selection for both CIP resistance and increased growth is eliminated.
source: As TGC eclipses acritical concentration of approximately 0.025 g/mL, selection for both CIP resistance and increased growth is eliminated.
evidence: This is a specific result from the model and experimental comparison.

claim: Comparisons between the model and experiment involve no adjustable parameters.
source: We note that comparisons between the model and experiment involve no adjustable parameters, and while the model captures the qualitative trends, it slightly but systematically underestimates the growth across TGC concentrations – perhaps suggesting additional evolutionary dynamics not captured by the model.
evidence: This is a statement about the model validation approach and its limitations.

claim: The model slightly but systematically underestimates the growth across TGC concentrations, perhaps suggesting additional evolutionary dynamics not captured by the model.
source: We note that comparisons between the model and experiment involve no adjustable parameters, and while the model captures the qualitative trends, it slightly but systematically underestimates the growth across TGC concentrations – perhaps suggesting additional evolutionary dynamics not captured by the model.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the model based on comparison with experimental data.

claim: The experimental results can be explained by the strongly antagonistic interaction between TGC and CIP, which reverses the selection for resistance to CIP at sufficiently high TGC concentrations.
source: Intuitively, the experimental results can be explained by the strongly antagonistic interaction between the two drugs, which reverses the selection for resistance to CIP at sufficiently high TGC concentrations (compare CIP resistance at TGC = 0 and TGC = 0.04 g/mL, which both involve CIP ≈ 0.2 g/mL; similar results have been seen in other species and for other drug combinations; Chait et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The model captures the qualitative features of both resistance changes to the component drugs and growth adaptation for two additional drug pairs.
source: We also compared model predictions with experimental adaptation to two additional drug pairs (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2) and again found that the model captures the qualitative features of both resistance changes to the component drugs and growth adaptation.
evidence: This is a result from comparing model predictions with experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The model can be extended to include mutation events linking different phenotypes.
source: While we have focused on selection dynamics, the model can be extended to include mutation events linking different phenotypes (i.e., linking different pairs of scaling parameters).
evidence: This is stated as an extension of the model.

claim: Mutational pathways may be necessary to capture certain evolutionary features such as historical contingencies between sequentially acquired mutations.
source: These mutational pathways may be necessary to capture certain evolutionary features – for example, historical contingencies between sequentially acquired mutations (Barbosa et al., 2017; Card et al., 2019; Das et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When mutations occur with uniform probability between the ancestral strain and each mutant, the evolutionary dynamics are qualitatively similar to those in the absence of mutation.
source: When the mutation matrix has a particularly simple structure, the effects of mutation will be similar to those of selection. For example, when mutations occur with uniform probability between the ancestral strain and each mutant, the evolutionary dynamics are qualitatively similar to those in the absence of mutation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, compare to Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Certain mutational structures can lead to new behavior compared to selection-only dynamics.
source: On the other hand, certain mutational structures can lead to new behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about the effects of mutational structure.

claim: The sequential pathway leads to slower adaptation of growth as the population evolves first toward the most fit single mutant before eventually arriving at the double-resistant phenotype.
source: While both mutational structures lead eventually to a population of double-resistant phenotypes (RR), the sequential pathway leads to slower adaptation of growth as the population evolves first toward the most fit single mutant (in this case, RS because the drug combination contains a higher concentration of drug 1) before eventually arriving at RR (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The specific trajectory depends on both the drug interaction (the shape of the growth contours) and the specific dosage combination.
source: The specific trajectory will of course depend on both the drug interaction (the shape of the growth contours) and the specific dosage combination (see Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The model framework can be used to predict phenotypic evolution and growth dynamics in a bacterial population under consecutive treatments involving different dosage combinations of the same two drugs.
source: The model framework can be used to predict phenotypic evolution and growth dynamics in a bacterial population under consecutive treatments involving different dosage combinations of the same two drugs.
evidence: This is stated as an application of the model shown in Figure 7.

claim: The dynamics of resistance and growth changes depend on both the relative duration of each treatment and total treatment length in sequential therapies.
source: However, the dynamics of these changes depend on both the relative duration of each treatment and total treatment length (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 7 and supplementary figures.

claim: The resistance to each drug and the growth rate increase monotonically as the fraction of time in treatment B increases for a fixed total treatment length.
source: If we vary the relative length of the two epochs while keeping the total treatment length fixed, we find that the resistance to each drug and the growth rate increase monotonically as the fraction of time in B increases (Figure 7H–J).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: The effects of a two-epoch (A then B) treatment cannot be inferred as a simple linear interpolation between the effects of A-only and B-only treatments.
source: It is notable, however, that effects (both resistance levels and final growth) change nonlinearly as the fraction of time in B is increased – that is, even in this simple model, the effects of a two-epoch (A then B) treatment cannot be inferred as a simple linear interpolation between the effects of A-only and B-only treatments.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results on sequential treatments.

claim: The results provide a unified framework for incorporating both drug interactions and collateral effects to predict phenotypic adaptation on coarse-grained fitness landscapes.
source: Our results provide a unified framework for incorporating both drug interactions and collateral effects to predict phenotypic adaptation on coarse-grained fitness landscapes that are measurable features of the ancestral population (Table 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: Special cases of the model reproduce previous experimental results that appear to be contradictory.
source: Special cases of the model reproduce previous experimental results that appear, on the surface, to be contradictory; indeed, adaptation can be driven primarily by drug interactions, primarily by collateral effects, or by a combination of both, and the balance of these effects can be shifted using tunable properties of the system (i.e., the ratio of drug dosages).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the model's ability to reconcile different experimental observations.

claim: The model was inspired by rescaling arguments originally introduced in Chait et al., 2007 and shown to capture phenotypic features of dose-response surfaces or adaptation in multiple bacterial species.
source: Our model was inspired by rescaling arguments that were originally introduced in Chait et al., 2007 and have since been shown to capture phenotypic features of dose-response surfaces or adaptation in multiple bacterial species (Michel et al., 2008; Hegreness et al., 2008; Torella et al., 2010; Wood and Cluzel, 2012; Wood et al., 2014; Dean et al., 2020; Das et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The results complement prior studies by showing how rescaling assumptions, when formalized in a population dynamics model, lead to testable predictions for the dynamics of both growth adaptation and phenotype evolution.
source: Our results complement these studies by showing how similar rescaling assumptions, when formalized in a population dynamics model, lead to testable predictions for the dynamics of both growth adaptation and phenotype (resistance) evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the study relative to prior work.

claim: The model has a simple intuitive explanation, with evolutionary trajectories driven by weighted gradient dynamics on two-dimensional landscapes.
source: Importantly, the model also has a simple intuitive explanation, with evolutionary trajectories driven by weighted gradient dynamics on two-dimensional landscapes, where the local geometry of the landscape reflects the drug interaction and collateral effects constrain the direction of motion.
evidence: This is a summary of the conceptual insight provided by the model.

claim: De novo mutation can be integrated in the same framework, provided the mutational structure among a pool of possible phenotypes is known or if specific assumptions are made.
source: We have also illustrated how de novo mutation can be integrated in the same framework, provided the mutational structure among a pool of possible phenotypes is known or if specific assumptions are made regarding functional links and constraints for shifts between different resistance levels.
evidence: This is a statement about the extensibility of the model.

claim: Mutation at constant rate is a classic version of the complete Price equation.
source: Mutation at constant rate is indeed a classic version of the complete Price equation.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between the model and the Price equation.

claim: More complex mutational effects, including stress-dependent modulation of mutation rate, could be included as a more flexible tunable term in Equation 5.
source: However, more complex mutational effects – including stress-dependent modulation of mutation rate (Kohanski et al., 2010; Vasse et al., 2020) – could be included as a more flexible tunable term in Equation 5.
evidence: This is a statement about potential extensions of the model, supported by citations.

claim: The approach has pedagogical value as it connects evolutionary effects of drug combinations and collateral effects with well-established concepts in evolutionary biology and population genetics.
source: Our approach also has pedagogical value as it connects evolutionary effects of drug combinations and collateral effects with well-established concepts in evolutionary biology and population genetics (Price, 1970; Price, 1972; Day and Gandon, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the broader value of the approach, supported by citations.

claim: Approximations similar to Equation 9 have been derived previously in quantitative genetics models and other applications of the Price equation.
source: Approximations similar to Equation 9 have been derived previously in quantitative genetics models (Abrams et al., 1993; Taylor, 1996) and other applications of the Price equation (Lehtonen, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When the gradient vanishes, the point corresponds to a singular point or an evolutionarily singular strategy.
source: when the gradient vanishes, this point corresponds to a singular point (Waxman and Gavrilets, 2005) or an evolutionarily singular strategy (Geritz et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in evolutionary theory.

claim: Whether a singular point may be reached (convergence stability) and how much variance in trait values can be maintained around such point (whether evolutionarily stable) depend on higher-order derivatives.
source: Whether such point may be reached (convergence stability) and how much variance in trait values can be maintained around such point (whether evolutionarily stable [ESS]) depend on other features, such as higher-order derivatives (Otto and Day, 2011; Eshel et al., 1997; Lehtonen, 2018; Smith, 1982; Parker and Smith, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in evolutionary theory.

claim: Whether the point (0,0) is reachable depends on the available mutants preexisting at very low frequencies in the population, or on the speed and biases in the mutational process.
source: However, whether that point is reachable in general or within a given time frame will depend on the available mutants preexisting at very low frequencies in the population, or on the speed and biases in the mutational process itself, if such mutants are to be generated de novo during treatment.
evidence: This is an explanation of factors that determine evolutionary outcomes.

claim: The model allows for long-term coexistence between different strains when the rescaled effective drug concentrations experienced by both strains fall along a single contour of constant growth.
source: In principle, the model also allows for long-term coexistence between different strains; in that case, the rescaled effective drug concentrations experienced by both strains would fall along a single contour of constant growth.
evidence: This is a statement about a possible outcome in the model.

claim: While variance in the population growth will necessarily decrease over time, variance in the traits (scaling parameters) themselves can change non-monotonically.
source: Hence, while variance in the population growth will necessarily decrease over time, variance in the traits (scaling parameters) themselves can change non-monotonically.
evidence: This is a statement about the dynamics of trait variance in the model.

claim: The framework is sufficiently flexible to integrate different strands of empirical data.
source: The framework is sufficiently flexible to integrate different strands of empirical data, and our results underscore the need for quantitative phenotype data tracking resistance to multiple drugs simultaneously, especially when drug combinations are potentially driving selection dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the framework.

claim: The results underscore the need for quantitative phenotype data tracking resistance to multiple drugs simultaneously.
source: The framework is sufficiently flexible to integrate different strands of empirical data, and our results underscore the need for quantitative phenotype data tracking resistance to multiple drugs simultaneously, especially when drug combinations are potentially driving selection dynamics.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: The dominant approach in describing resistance at an epidemiological level has been to use fixed breakpoints in MIC and track the percentage of isolates above or below such breakpoint.
source: At an epidemiological level, the dominant approach in describing resistance has been to use fixed breakpoints in MIC and track the percentage of isolates with MIC above (drug-resistant) or below (drug-sensitive) such breakpoint (e.g., ECDC, 2019; Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological reports.

claim: By missing or decoupling patterns of co-occurrence between MICs to different drugs across isolates, the binary breakpoint approach remains incomplete for mechanistic predictions.
source: By missing or decoupling patterns of co-occurrence between MICs to different drugs across isolates, this approach remains incomplete for mechanistic predictions.
evidence: This is a critique of current epidemiological approaches based on the insights from the model.

claim: The framework suggests that going beyond binary description towards a more continuous and multidimensional phenotype characterization of drug resistance is possible.
source: Our framework suggests that going beyond such binary description towards a more continuous and multidimensional phenotype characterization of drug resistance is possible, with applications not just in microbiology but also in the evolutionary epidemiology of drug resistance (Day and Gandon, 2012; Day et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study, supported by citations.

claim: These advances may yield better and more precise predictions of resistance evolution at multiple scales, and optimized treatments that balance short-term inhibitory effects with longer-term evolutionary consequences.
source: In the long run, these advances may yield better and more precise predictions of resistance evolution at multiple scales, and, in turn, optimized treatments that balance short-term inhibitory effects of a drug cocktail with its inseparable, longer-term evolutionary consequences.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential future impact of the approach.

claim: The approach provides a low-dimensional approximation to the high-dimensional dynamics governing the evolution of resistance.
source: Perhaps most importantly, our approach provides a low-dimensional approximation to the high-dimensional dynamics governing the evolution of resistance.
evidence: This is a summary of a key feature of the approach.

claim: The model uses rescaling arguments to connect measurable traits of resistant cells (scaling parameters) to environment-dependent phenotypes (growth).
source: In contrast to the classical genotype-centric approaches to resistance, our model uses rescaling arguments to connect measurable traits of resistant cells (scaling parameters) to environment-dependent phenotypes (growth).
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: This rescaling dramatically reduces the complexity of the problem as the two-drug-response surfaces can be estimated from only single-drug dose-response curves.
source: This rescaling dramatically reduces the complexity of the problem as the two-drug-response surfaces – and, effectively, the fitness landscape – can be estimated from only single-drug dose-response curves.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical advantage of the rescaling approach.

claim: Coarse-grained models can help extract simplifying principles from otherwise intractable complexity.
source: Such coarse-grained models can help extract simplifying principles from otherwise intractable complexity (Shoval et al., 2012; Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Price equation formalism reveals links between trait-fitness covariance and selection that are already embedded in simple models of population growth.
source: In many ways, the classical Price equation performs a similar function, revealing links between trait-fitness covariance and selection that, at a mathematical level, are already embedded in simple models of population growth.
evidence: This is a statement about the conceptual value of the Price equation.

claim: In the case of multidrug resistance, the formalism reveals that drug interactions and collateral effects are not independent features of resistance evolution.
source: In the case of multidrug resistance, this formalism reveals that drug interactions and collateral effects are not independent features of resistance evolution, and neither, alone, can provide a complete picture.
evidence: This is a key conceptual insight from the study.

claim: Drug interactions and collateral effects are coupled through local geometry of the two-drug-response surface.
source: Instead, they are coupled through local geometry of the two-drug-response surface, and we show how specific dosage combinations can shift the weighting of these two effects, providing a framework for systematic optimization of time-dependent multidrug therapies.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: Specific dosage combinations can shift the weighting of drug interactions and collateral effects, providing a framework for systematic optimization of time-dependent multidrug therapies.
source: Instead, they are coupled through local geometry of the two-drug-response surface, and we show how specific dosage combinations can shift the weighting of these two effects, providing a framework for systematic optimization of time-dependent multidrug therapies.
evidence: This is a key finding and potential application of the study.

claim: The scaling parameters for a given mutant can be directly estimated by comparing single-drug dose-response curves of the mutant and ancestral populations.
source: The scaling parameters for a given mutant can be directly estimated by comparing single-drug dose-response curves of the mutant and ancestral populations.
evidence: This is a description of the method for estimating model parameters.

claim: It is not clear a priori which isolates are present at time 0 of any given evolution experiment.
source: While it is straightforward to estimate the scaling parameters for any particular isolate, it is not clear a priori which isolates are present at time 0 of any given evolution experiment.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation in applying the model to experiments.

claim: To compare predictions with lab evolution experiments, scaling parameters were estimated for all isolates collected during lab evolution experiments in each drug pair.
source: To compare predictions of our model with lab evolution experiments, we first estimated scaling parameters for all isolates collected during lab evolution experiments in each drug pair (Dean et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the method for model validation.

claim: The ensemble of isolates includes 50–100 isolates per drug combination collected at different timepoints and selected in different dosage combinations.
source: This ensemble includes 50–100 isolates per drug combination and includes isolates collected at different timepoints during the evolution (after days 1, 2, or 3) as well as isolates selected in different dosage combinations Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data used.

claim: Scaling parameters were randomly sampled from the ensemble to generate low-level standing diversity at time 0 for each simulation.
source: We then randomly sampled from this ensemble to generate low-level standing diversity (on average, approximately 10 distinct pairs of scaling parameters) at time 0 for each simulation of the model, and we repeated this subsampling 100 times to generate an ensemble of evolutionary trajectories for each condition.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation method.

claim: The results of the simulation can, in principle, depend on how the scaling parameters are sampled.
source: The results of the simulation can, in principle, depend on how these scaling parameters are sampled.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential limitation of the simulation approach.

claim: The qualitative differences between simulations do not depend heavily on the choice of subsampling in the data used.
source: While the qualitative differences between simulations do not depend heavily on this choice of subsampling in the data used here (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), one can imagine scenarios where details of the subsampling significantly impact the outcome.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the results, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Precise comparison with experiment requires accurate estimates for the total evolutionary time and for the initial frequency of all resistant mutants.
source: Similarly, precise comparison with experiment requires accurate estimates for the total evolutionary time and for the initial frequency of all resistant mutants, though for these data the qualitative results do not depend sensitively on these choices (Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a statement about requirements for model validation, supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The limitations in comparing model with experiment are not fundamental limitations of the model itself, but arise because of imprecise measures of the standing variation.
source: We stress that these are not fundamental limitations of the model itself, but instead arise because we do not have a precise measure of the standing variation characterizing these particular experiments.
evidence: This is a clarification about the source of uncertainty in model validation.

claim: A more accurate ensemble of scaling parameters could be inferred from cleverly designed fluctuation tests or from high-throughput, single-cell phenotypic studies.
source: In principle, a more accurate ensemble of scaling parameters could be inferred from cleverly designed fluctuation tests (Luria and Delbrück, 1943) or, ideally, from high-throughput, single-cell phenotypic studies (Baltekin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experimental approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Subsampling could be modulated to simulate the effects of different effective population sizes, with standing diversity expected to be significantly larger for large populations.
source: At a theoretical level, subsampling could also be modulated to simulate the effects of different effective population sizes, with standing diversity expected to be significantly larger for large populations.
evidence: This is a statement about how the model could be extended.

claim: The primary rescaling assumption of the model is that growth of a drug-resistant mutant is well approximated by growth of the ancestral strain at a new 'effective' drug concentration.
source: The primary rescaling assumption of the model is that growth of a drug-resistant mutant is well approximated by growth of the ancestral strain at a new 'effective' drug concentration – one that differs from the true external concentration.
evidence: This is a restatement of the fundamental model assumption.

claim: The rescaling approximation has considerable empirical support.
source: This approximation has considerable empirical support (Chait et al., 2007; Wood and Cluzel, 2012; Wood et al., 2014; Das et al., 2020) but is not expected to always hold
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rescaling approximation is not expected to always hold; there are examples where mutations lead to more complex nonlinear transformations of the drug-response surface.
source: This approximation has considerable empirical support (Chait et al., 2007; Wood and Cluzel, 2012; Wood et al., 2014; Das et al., 2020) but is not expected to always hold; indeed, there are examples where mutations lead to more complex nonlinear transformations of the drug-response surface (Wood et al., 2014; Munck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the model, supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that selection can act on some other feature of the dose-response curve, such as modulating its steepness.
source: In addition, it is possible that selection can act on some other feature of the dose-response curve characterizing single-drug effects – modulating, for example, its steepness (rather than merely its scale).
evidence: This is a statement about a potential limitation of the model.

claim: The model has neglected a number of features that may impact microbial evolution, including clonal interference, intercellular or intra-lineage competition, cooperation, and effects of demographic noise and population extinction.
source: For simplicity, we have also neglected a number of features that may impact microbial evolution. For example, we have assumed that different subpopulations grow exponentially, neglecting potential interactions including clonal interference (Gerrish and Lenski, 1998), intercellular (Koch et al., 2014; Hansen et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2020) or intra-lineage (Ogbunugafor and Eppstein, 2017) competition, and cooperation (Yurtsev et al., 2013; Sorg et al., 2016; Estrela and Brown, 2018; Frost et al., 2018; Hallinen et al., 2020), as well as potential effects of demographic noise and population extinction (Coates et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the model, supported by citations.

claim: These complexities could be incorporated in the model, perhaps at the expense of some intuitive interpretations.
source: These complexities could also be incorporated in our model, perhaps at the expense of some intuitive interpretations (e.g., weighted gradient dynamics) that currently apply.
evidence: This is a statement about potential extensions of the model.

claim: The model has not explicitly included a fitness cost of resistance.
source: In addition, we have not explicitly included a fitness cost of resistance (Andersson and Hughes, 2010) – that is, we assume that growth rates of mutants and ancestral cells are identical in the absence of drug.
evidence: This is a statement about a simplifying assumption of the model, with a citation.

claim: While fitness costs have traditionally been seen as essential for reversing resistance, the results underscore that reversing adaptation relies on differential fitness along a multidimensional continuum of environments, not merely binary conditions.
source: While such fitness costs have traditionally been seen as essential for reversing resistance (with, e.g., drug-free 'holidays'; Dunai et al., 2019), our results underscore the idea that reversing adaptation relies on differential fitness along a multidimensional continuum of environments, not merely binary (drug/no drug) conditions.
evidence: This is a conceptual insight from the study, with a citation.

claim: The results indicate resistance and bacterial growth can be significantly constrained by optimal tuning of multidrug environments, even in the absence of fitness cost.
source: Our results indicate resistance and bacterial growth can be significantly constrained by optimal tuning of multidrug environments, even in the absence of fitness cost.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: The model deals only with heritable resistance and may not capture phenotypic effects associated with transient resistance or cellular hysteresis.
source: Finally, our model deals only with heritable resistance and therefore may not capture phenotypic affects associated with, for example, transient resistance (El Meouche and Dunlop, 2018) or cellular hysteresis (Roemhild et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the model, supported by citations.

claim: The goal was to strike a balance between analytical tractability and generality vs. biological realism and system specificity.
source: Our goal was to strike a balance between analytical tractability and generality vs. biological realism and system specificity.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling philosophy.

claim: The predictions of the model depend on properties of the dose-response surfaces, the collection of scaling parameters, and the specific mutational structure.
source: But we stress that the predictions of this model do not come for free; they depend, for example, on properties of the dose-response surfaces, the collection of scaling parameters, and the specific mutational structure.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for making predictions with the model.

claim: In many cases, the features required for model predictions can be determined empirically; in other cases, some or all of these properties may be unknown.
source: In many cases, these features can be determined empirically; in other cases, some or all of these properties may be unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical applicability of the model.

claim: The evolutionary predictions of the model will ultimately depend on the inputs, and it is difficult to draw general conclusions that apply across all classes of drug combinations, collateral effects, and mutational structures.
source: The evolutionary predictions of the model will ultimately depend on these inputs, and it is difficult to draw general conclusions (e.g., 'synergistic combinations always accelerate resistance') that apply across all classes of drug combinations, collateral effects, and mutational structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of generalizing from the model.

claim: The framework is valuable because it generates testable predictions in situations that might otherwise seem intractably complex.
source: But we believe the framework is valuable precisely because it generates testable predictions in situations that might otherwise seem intractably complex.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the framework.
